papers_seen.author: Hurst
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Practices in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques have matured into a diverse set of methods for producing smaller, faster, and sometimes more robust models from larger teachers. Approaches span from soft-label and internal-representation transfer to data-free distillation, federated/distilled training for privacy and communication efficiency, and task-adaptive architecture search for large pretrained language models. Empirical work shows KD can improve inference efficiency with limited accuracy loss, transfer adversarial robustness, and enable effective low-precision and task-specific compressed models, while theoretical analyses and algorithmic variants clarify when and why distillation helps.

papers_seen.author: Johnson
papers_seen.title: Methods and Practices for Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible set of techniques to transfer knowledge from a high-capacity teacher model to a smaller, faster, or otherwise constrained student. Work across modalities and tasks has shown KD can yield compact models that approach teacher performance, enable deployment on resource-limited devices, help mitigate data-availability or privacy constraints, and act as a vehicle for transferring ensemble or multi-teacher knowledge into a single model. Practical KD methods vary in what they transfer (logits, intermediate features, or rankings), whether they require original training data, and how they structure training (offline, online, adversarial, or curriculum-based). Empirical and methodological work highlights (1) the effectiveness of feature-level supervision in many settings, (2) the value of synthetic or replayed data when real data are unavailable, (3) that ensemble and online schemes can speed training and improve robustness, and (4) that augmentation, sample selection, and task-specific losses materially affect distilled-student outcomes.

papers_seen.author: Jones
papers_seen.title: Practical Principles for Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and model compression are practical, broadly applicable strategies for deploying large deep models in resource-constrained settings. Across tasks from retrieval and reading comprehension to multimodal generation and federated learning, distillation can preserve much of a teacher model's performance while cutting inference cost, enabling new real-time and on-device applications. Success depends less on a single canonical recipe and more on matching the distillation strategy to the deployment constraints and task: progressive structural compression, task-adaptive architecture search, layer- and feature-aware matching, careful treatment of soft targets and data, and privacy- or communication-aware protocols each address common real-world failure modes. Combining these complementary techniques yields compact students that are both efficient and robust for NLP and other domains.

papers_seen.author: Hahn
papers_seen.title: PKD: General Distillation Framework for Object Detectors via Pearson Correlation Coefficient
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation(KD) is a widely-used technique to train compact models in object detection. However, there is still a lack of study on how to distill between heterogeneous detectors. In this paper, we empirically find that better FPN features from a heterogeneous teacher detector can help the student although their detection heads and label assignments are different. However, directly aligning the feature maps to distill detectors suffers from two problems. First, the difference in feature magnitude between the teacher and the student could enforce overly strict constraints on the student. Second, the FPN stages and channels with large feature magnitude from the teacher model could dominate the gradient of distillation loss, which will overwhelm the effects of other features in KD and introduce much noise. To address the above issues, we propose to imitate features with Pearson Correlation Coefficient to focus on the relational information from the teacher and relax constraints on the magnitude of the features. Our method consistently outperforms the existing detection KD methods and works for both homogeneous and heterogeneous student-teacher pairs. Furthermore, it converges faster. With a powerful MaskRCNN-Swin detector as the teacher, ResNet-50 based RetinaNet and FCOS achieve 41.5% and 43.9% mAP on COCO2017, which are 4.1\% and 4.8\% higher than the baseline, respectively.

papers_seen.author: Decker
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression: Practical Effectiveness, Theoretical Trade-offs, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has emerged as a practical and flexible approach to compressing large neural networks while retaining much of their predictive power. Across modalities and tasks—NLP, vision, recommendation, graph learning, and generative modeling—KD-based methods enable faster inference and lower resource use with modest accuracy loss. However, realizing these gains requires attention to teacher quality, the form of supervisory signal (soft vs. hard labels), data augmentation and curriculum, and task-adaptive design. KD can be combined with other compression techniques (pruning, architecture search) and adapted for privacy-preserving or distributed settings. This paper argues that KD is a broadly applicable core strategy for model compression, outlines the mechanisms that make it effective, and provides practical recommendations grounded in empirical and theoretical findings.

papers_seen.author: Valencia
papers_seen.title: Compression of Deep Learning Models for Text: A Survey
papers_seen.abstract: In recent years, the fields of natural language processing (NLP) and information retrieval (IR) have made tremendous progress thanksto deep learning models like Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs), Gated Recurrent Units (GRUs) and Long Short-Term Memory (LSTMs)networks, and Transformer [120] based models like Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT) [24], GenerativePre-training Transformer (GPT-2) [94], Multi-task Deep Neural Network (MT-DNN) [73], Extra-Long Network (XLNet) [134], Text-to-text transfer transformer (T5) [95], T-NLG [98] and GShard [63]. But these models are humongous in size. On the other hand,real world applications demand small model size, low response times and low computational power wattage. In this survey, wediscuss six different types of methods (Pruning, Quantization, Knowledge Distillation, Parameter Sharing, Tensor Decomposition, andSub-quadratic Transformer based methods) for compression of such models to enable their deployment in real industry NLP projects.Given the critical need of building applications with efficient and small models, and the large amount of recently published work inthis area, we believe that this survey organizes the plethora of work done by the 'deep learning for NLP' community in the past fewyears and presents it as a coherent story.

papers_seen.author: Rhodes
papers_seen.title: Lifelong Language Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: It is challenging to perform lifelong language learning (LLL) on a stream of different tasks without any performance degradation comparing to the multi-task counterparts. To address this issue, we present Lifelong Language Knowledge Distillation (L2KD), a simple but efficient method that can be easily applied to existing LLL architectures in order to mitigate the degradation. Specifically, when the LLL model is trained on a new task, we assign a teacher model to first learn the new task, and pass the knowledge to the LLL model via knowledge distillation. Therefore, the LLL model can better adapt to the new task while keeping the previously learned knowledge. Experiments show that the proposed L2KD consistently improves previous state-of-the-art models, and the degradation comparing to multi-task models in LLL tasks is well mitigated for both sequence generation and text classification tasks.

papers_seen.author: Rodriguez
papers_seen.title: Extract the Knowledge of Graph Neural Networks and Go Beyond it: An Effective Knowledge Distillation Framework
papers_seen.abstract: Semi-supervised learning on graphs is an important problem in the machine learning area. In recent years, state-of-the-art classification methods based on graph neural networks (GNNs) have shown their superiority over traditional ones such as label propagation. However, the sophisticated architectures of these neural models will lead to a complex prediction mechanism, which could not make full use of valuable prior knowledge lying in the data, e.g., structurally correlated nodes tend to have the same class. In this paper, we propose a framework based on knowledge distillation to address the above issues. Our framework extracts the knowledge of an arbitrary learned GNN model (teacher model), and injects it into a well-designed student model. The student model is built with two simple prediction mechanisms, i.e., label propagation and feature transformation, which naturally preserves structure-based and feature-based prior knowledge, respectively. In specific, we design the student model as a trainable combination of parameterized label propagation and feature transformation modules. As a result, the learned student can benefit from both prior knowledge and the knowledge in GNN teachers for more effective predictions. Moreover, the learned student model has a more interpretable prediction process than GNNs. We conduct experiments on five public benchmark datasets and employ seven GNN models including GCN, GAT, APPNP, SAGE, SGC, GCNII and GLP as the teacher models. Experimental results show that the learned student model can consistently outperform its corresponding teacher model by 1.4% - 4.7% on average. Code and data are available at https://github.com/BUPT-GAMMA/CPF

papers_seen.author: Chavez
papers_seen.title: Practical Principles for Effective Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable approach to compress large models into smaller, efficient students while retaining much of the teacher's performance. Empirical and methodological advances show KD succeeds when (1) the teacher signals are adapted to student capacity, (2) internal representations and attention patterns are aligned when architectures differ, and (3) distillation is combined with complementary compression methods (pruning, low-precision, pretraining) and task-aware training regimes. This paper argues that KD should be treated as a flexible toolbox rather than a single recipe: carefully chosen losses, multi-source reliability estimation, feature-level objectives, and integration with pretraining or hardware-aware compression yield the best trade-offs between model size, speed, and accuracy across vision, language, and graph domains.

papers_seen.author: Maddox
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core Strategy for Compression, Regularization and Privacy-Preserving Transfer
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and flexible approach for compressing high-capacity models into lightweight students while preserving or even improving generalization. Beyond simple teacher–student logits matching, KD can transfer architectural inductive biases, act as an effective regularizer, enable compression without access to original training data, and be adapted to low-data and multi-teacher settings. The choice of distillation objective, the availability of data, and the reliability of teacher signals determine success; consequently, a portfolio of techniques (data synthesis, augmentation, calibrated divergences, and confidence-aware aggregation) is needed to make KD robust and widely applicable in deep learning and NLP deployments.

papers_seen.author: Hoffman
papers_seen.title: Federated Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Distributed learning frameworks often rely on exchanging model parameters across workers, instead of revealing their raw data. A prime example is federated learning that exchanges the gradients or weights of each neural network model. Under limited communication resources, however, such a method becomes extremely costly particularly for modern deep neural networks having a huge number of model parameters. In this regard, federated distillation (FD) is a compelling distributed learning solution that only exchanges the model outputs whose dimensions are commonly much smaller than the model sizes (e.g., 10 labels in the MNIST dataset). The goal of this chapter is to provide a deep understanding of FD while demonstrating its communication efficiency and applicability to a variety of tasks. To this end, towards demystifying the operational principle of FD, the first part of this chapter provides a novel asymptotic analysis for two foundational algorithms of FD, namely knowledge distillation (KD) and co-distillation (CD), by exploiting the theory of neural tangent kernel (NTK). Next, the second part elaborates on a baseline implementation of FD for a classification task, and illustrates its performance in terms of accuracy and communication efficiency compared to FL. Lastly, to demonstrate the applicability of FD to various distributed learning tasks and environments, the third part presents two selected applications, namely FD over asymmetric uplink-and-downlink wireless channels and FD for reinforcement learning.

papers_seen.author: Richards
papers_seen.title: TextKD-GAN: Text Generation using KnowledgeDistillation and Generative Adversarial Networks
papers_seen.abstract: Text generation is of particular interest in many NLP applications such as machine translation, language modeling, and text summarization. Generative adversarial networks (GANs) achieved a remarkable success in high quality image generation in computer vision,and recently, GANs have gained lots of interest from the NLP community as well. However, achieving similar success in NLP would be more challenging due to the discrete nature of text. In this work, we introduce a method using knowledge distillation to effectively exploit GAN setup for text generation. We demonstrate how autoencoders (AEs) can be used for providing a continuous representation of sentences, which is a smooth representation that assign non-zero probabilities to more than one word. We distill this representation to train the generator to synthesize similar smooth representations. We perform a number of experiments to validate our idea using different datasets and show that our proposed approach yields better performance in terms of the BLEU score and Jensen-Shannon distance (JSD) measure compared to traditional GAN-based text generation approaches without pre-training.

papers_seen.author: Rios
papers_seen.title: Improving Neural Topic Models using Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Topic models are often used to identify human-interpretable topics to help make sense of large document collections. We use knowledge distillation to combine the best attributes of probabilistic topic models and pretrained transformers. Our modular method can be straightforwardly applied with any neural topic model to improve topic quality, which we demonstrate using two models having disparate architectures, obtaining state-of-the-art topic coherence. We show that our adaptable framework not only improves performance in the aggregate over all estimated topics, as is commonly reported, but also in head-to-head comparisons of aligned topics.

papers_seen.author: Gaines
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and model compression techniques enable the deployment of state-of-the-art deep learning models in resource-constrained environments by transferring knowledge from larger teacher models to smaller, more efficient student models. These approaches have demonstrated significant success across diverse applications including natural language processing, computer vision, and speech processing, achieving substantial reductions in model size and computational cost while maintaining competitive accuracy levels. This synthesis explores the diverse methodologies, theoretical foundations, and practical applications of knowledge distillation and compression techniques in modern deep learning systems.

papers_seen.author: Mcclain
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation in Deep Learning and NLP: Powerful, Practical, but Not a Panacea
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has become a core technique for compressing large models, transferring knowledge across architectures, enabling private or federated workflows, and improving efficiency for deployment in resource-constrained settings. While KD often yields substantial practical gains—reducing model size and inference cost with limited loss in performance—it has important theoretical and empirical limitations related to optimization, data dependence, model and domain heterogeneity, and teacher–student mismatch. A pragmatic stance recognizes KD as a versatile toolset whose effectiveness depends on how it is applied: the choice of distilled targets (logits, features, or relations), the availability or synthesis of data, the use of multiple teachers or staged procedures, and awareness of when distillation can harm or help generalization. This paper argues that KD should be used as part of a broader compression and adaptation strategy guided by empirical diagnostics and appropriate extensions (multi-teacher, zero-shot/data-free, federated/distilled protocols, or self-supervised distillation) rather than as an off-the-shelf cure-all.

papers_seen.author: Lynch
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning: Transferring Knowledge for Efficient Neural Networks
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a powerful technique for compressing large neural networks into smaller, more efficient models while maintaining performance. This approach transfers knowledge from a larger teacher model to a smaller student model, enabling deployment on resource-constrained devices. Model compression through distillation has proven effective across diverse applications including natural language processing, computer vision, and multimodal learning. This paper surveys the principles, methods, and applications of knowledge distillation and related compression techniques in deep learning.

papers_seen.author: Adams
papers_seen.title: Practical Paths and Limits for Knowledge Distillation in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) remains a central technique for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students while preserving performance. KD has evolved from simple logit matching to diverse strategies that address data availability, task specificity, representation-level transfer, and architectural mismatches. However, fundamental limits—especially under heterogeneous data or federated settings—and practical challenges such as selecting useful teacher signal and coping with student capacity remain. A pragmatic approach combines data-aware or data-free sample generation, representation- and layer-level objectives, and task-aware filtering to maximize transfer while respecting privacy, compute, and deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Perez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and Natural Language Processing
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a widely-adopted technique for compressing neural networks by transferring knowledge from a larger teacher model to a smaller student model. This approach enables the development of efficient models with reduced parameters and computational requirements while maintaining high performance across various domains including computer vision and natural language processing. The field has evolved to encompass diverse methodologies, from basic logit matching to advanced layer-wise and feature-level distillation approaches, with applications spanning machine translation, question answering, sentiment analysis, and multi-modal learning.

papers_seen.author: Davis
papers_seen.title: Feature-map-level Online Adversarial Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Feature maps contain rich information about image intensity and spatial correlation. However, previous online knowledge distillation methods only utilize the class probabilities. Thus in this paper, we propose an online knowledge distillation method that transfers not only the knowledge of the class probabilities but also that of the feature map using the adversarial training framework. We train multiple networks simultaneously by employing discriminators to distinguish the feature map distributions of different networks. Each network has its corresponding discriminator which discriminates the feature map from its own as fake while classifying that of the other network as real. By training a network to fool the corresponding discriminator, it can learn the other network's feature map distribution. We show that our method performs better than the conventional direct alignment method such as L1 and is more suitable for online distillation. Also, we propose a novel cyclic learning scheme for training more than two networks together. We have applied our method to various network architectures on the classification task and discovered a significant improvement of performance especially in the case of training a pair of a small network and a large one.

papers_seen.author: Mayo
papers_seen.title: Rethinking Soft Labels for Knowledge Distillation: A Bias-Variance Tradeoff Perspective
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is an effective approach to leverage a well-trained network or an ensemble of them, named as the teacher, to guide the training of a student network. The outputs from the teacher network are used as soft labels for supervising the training of a new network. Recent studies \citep{muller2019does,yuan2020revisiting} revealed an intriguing property of the soft labels that making labels soft serves as a good regularization to the student network. From the perspective of statistical learning, regularization aims to reduce the variance, however how bias and variance change is not clear for training with soft labels. In this paper, we investigate the bias-variance tradeoff brought by distillation with soft labels. Specifically, we observe that during training the bias-variance tradeoff varies sample-wisely. Further, under the same distillation temperature setting, we observe that the distillation performance is negatively associated with the number of some specific samples, which are named as regularization samples since these samples lead to bias increasing and variance decreasing. Nevertheless, we empirically find that completely filtering out regularization samples also deteriorates distillation performance. Our discoveries inspired us to propose the novel weighted soft labels to help the network adaptively handle the sample-wise bias-variance tradeoff. Experiments on standard evaluation benchmarks validate the effectiveness of our method. Our code is available at \url{https://github.com/bellymonster/Weighted-Soft-Label-Distillation}.

papers_seen.author: Calderon
papers_seen.title: Learning Generalizable Models for Vehicle Routing Problems via Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Recent neural methods for vehicle routing problems always train and test the deep models on the same instance distribution (i.e., uniform). To tackle the consequent cross-distribution generalization concerns, we bring the knowledge distillation to this field and propose an Adaptive Multi-Distribution Knowledge Distillation (AMDKD) scheme for learning more generalizable deep models. Particularly, our AMDKD leverages various knowledge from multiple teachers trained on exemplar distributions to yield a light-weight yet generalist student model. Meanwhile, we equip AMDKD with an adaptive strategy that allows the student to concentrate on difficult distributions, so as to absorb hard-to-master knowledge more effectively. Extensive experimental results show that, compared with the baseline neural methods, our AMDKD is able to achieve competitive results on both unseen in-distribution and out-of-distribution instances, which are either randomly synthesized or adopted from benchmark datasets (i.e., TSPLIB and CVRPLIB). Notably, our AMDKD is generic, and consumes less computational resources for inference.

papers_seen.author: Wright
papers_seen.title: Distilled Semantics for Comprehensive Scene Understanding from Videos
papers_seen.abstract: Whole understanding of the surroundings is paramount to autonomous systems. Recent works have shown that deep neural networks can learn geometry (depth) and motion (optical flow) from a monocular video without any explicit supervision from ground truth annotations, particularly hard to source for these two tasks. In this paper, we take an additional step toward holistic scene understanding with monocular cameras by learning depth and motion alongside with semantics, with supervision for the latter provided by a pre-trained network distilling proxy ground truth images. We address the three tasks jointly by a) a novel training protocol based on knowledge distillation and self-supervision and b) a compact network architecture which enables efficient scene understanding on both power hungry GPUs and low-power embedded platforms. We thoroughly assess the performance of our framework and show that it yields state-of-the-art results for monocular depth estimation, optical flow and motion segmentation.

papers_seen.author: Alvarez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Applications, and Open Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression techniques produce compact models that retain much of the performance of larger teachers by transferring information during training. Approaches span logits-based distillation, feature and intermediate-layer matching, data-free or few-shot distillation, multi-teacher and task-aware strategies, and privacy-aware compression. Empirical studies reveal strengths (efficient deployment, competitive accuracy in many tasks) and limits (optimization gaps between teacher and student, sensitivity to data and training choices). Practical use in NLP and multimodal systems often combines multiple techniques (e.g., intermediate-layer alignment and feature mimicking) and benefits from teacher/teacher-ensemble design, but open issues remain around representation alignment, low-resource or private settings, and principled guarantees of fairness and generalization.

papers_seen.author: Hernandez
papers_seen.title: R2L: Distilling Neural Radiance Field to Neural Light Field for Efficient Novel View Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Recent research explosion on Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) shows the encouraging potential to represent complex scenes with neural networks. One major drawback of NeRF is its prohibitive inference time: Rendering a single pixel requires querying the NeRF network hundreds of times. To resolve it, existing efforts mainly attempt to reduce the number of required sampled points. However, the problem of iterative sampling still exists. On the other hand, Neural Light Field (NeLF) presents a more straightforward representation over NeRF in novel view synthesis -- the rendering of a pixel amounts to one single forward pass without ray-marching. In this work, we present a deep residual MLP network (88 layers) to effectively learn the light field. We show the key to successfully learning such a deep NeLF network is to have sufficient data, for which we transfer the knowledge from a pre-trained NeRF model via data distillation. Extensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world scenes show the merits of our method over other counterpart algorithms. On the synthetic scenes, we achieve 26-35x FLOPs reduction (per camera ray) and 28-31x runtime speedup, meanwhile delivering significantly better (1.4-2.8 dB average PSNR improvement) rendering quality than NeRF without any customized parallelism requirement.

papers_seen.author: Burton
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Research in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related model compression techniques enable deployment of large deep models in resource-constrained settings by transferring predictive behavior or internal representations from larger ‘‘teacher’’ models to smaller ‘‘student’’ models. Research over the past decade has developed multiple complementary approaches — logit-level distillation, feature- and attention-based imitation, architecture-aware compression, data-free and privacy-preserving variants, and teacher-training strategies — each addressing different practical constraints such as limited data, heterogeneous devices, latency, or privacy. Empirical work shows that careful design choices (what to transfer, when to transfer, and how to adapt student architectures) often determine whether a distilled student approaches teacher-level performance; theoretical and empirical analyses clarify when distillation helps, how ensemble and ‘‘dark knowledge’’ contribute, and why mixing hard and soft targets can be beneficial. Continued progress connects distillation with neural architecture search, meta-learning of teachers, and robust data synthesis to broaden applicability across vision, speech, retrieval, graph, and NLP tasks.

papers_seen.author: Liu
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning: Bridging Performance and Efficiency
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation has emerged as a powerful technique for model compression in deep learning, enabling the transfer of knowledge from large, computationally expensive models to smaller, more efficient ones. This approach addresses the critical challenge of deploying neural networks on resource-constrained devices while maintaining competitive performance. The technique applies across diverse domains including natural language processing, computer vision, and machine translation, demonstrating its versatility as a general-purpose compression method. By training smaller student models to mimic larger teacher models, knowledge distillation achieves significant reductions in model size and computational cost without substantial accuracy degradation, making it essential for practical deployment scenarios.

papers_seen.author: Robinson
papers_seen.title: Understanding and Improving Lexical Choice in Non-Autoregressive Translation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is essential for training non-autoregressive translation (NAT) models by reducing the complexity of the raw data with an autoregressive teacher model. In this study, we empirically show that as a side effect of this training, the lexical choice errors on low-frequency words are propagated to the NAT model from the teacher model. To alleviate this problem, we propose to expose the raw data to NAT models to restore the useful information of low-frequency words, which are missed in the distilled data. To this end, we introduce an extra Kullback-Leibler divergence term derived by comparing the lexical choice of NAT model and that embedded in the raw data. Experimental results across language pairs and model architectures demonstrate the effectiveness and universality of the proposed approach. Extensive analyses confirm our claim that our approach improves performance by reducing the lexical choice errors on low-frequency words. Encouragingly, our approach pushes the SOTA NAT performance on the WMT14 English-German and WMT16 Romanian-English datasets up to 27.8 and 33.8 BLEU points, respectively. The source code will be released.

papers_seen.author: Hodges
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Powerful Paradigm for Model Compression and Knowledge Transfer in Deep Learning
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation has emerged as a highly effective technique for compressing large neural networks into smaller, deployable models while maintaining competitive performance. This approach transfers learned representations from complex teacher networks to simpler student networks, enabling efficient model deployment across diverse applications. The technique has proven particularly valuable in natural language processing, computer vision, and speech recognition, where computational constraints often limit the use of state-of-the-art models. Beyond compression, knowledge distillation facilitates knowledge transfer across different model architectures, improves robustness, and supports learning from ensembles, making it an indispensable tool in modern deep learning.

papers_seen.author: Ellis
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Practices in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a widely used paradigm to compress large models into smaller, more efficient students by transferring information from teacher models. Research has explored multiple transfer mechanisms (soft labels, intermediate feature matching, layer mappings), teacher and data strategies (student-friendly teachers, multi-teacher weighting, data-free distillation, and data augmentation), and applied KD to a variety of tasks including BERT compression, non-autoregressive translation, and lightweight NLP models. Progress shows KD can preserve much of teacher performance while enabling substantial reductions in size and latency, but design choices about what to transfer, how teachers are trained, how data is constructed or augmented, and how multiple teachers are combined strongly affect outcomes. Remaining challenges include principled selection of transfer targets and data, robustness under domain shifts or heterogeneous deployments, and automating task-adaptive compression for downstream objectives.

papers_seen.author: Mason
papers_seen.title: Learning Student Networks via Feature Embedding
papers_seen.abstract: Deep convolutional neural networks have been widely used in numerous applications, but their demanding storage and computational resource requirements prevent their applications on mobile devices. Knowledge distillation aims to optimize a portable student network by taking the knowledge from a well-trained heavy teacher network. Traditional teacher-student based methods used to rely on additional fully-connected layers to bridge intermediate layers of teacher and student networks, which brings in a large number of auxiliary parameters. In contrast, this paper aims to propagate information from teacher to student without introducing new variables which need to be optimized. We regard the teacher-student paradigm from a new perspective of feature embedding. By introducing the locality preserving loss, the student network is encouraged to generate the low-dimensional features which could inherit intrinsic properties of their corresponding high-dimensional features from teacher network. The resulting portable network thus can naturally maintain the performance as that of the teacher network. Theoretical analysis is provided to justify the lower computation complexity of the proposed method. Experiments on benchmark datasets and well-trained networks suggest that the proposed algorithm is superior to state-of-the-art teacher-student learning methods in terms of computational and storage complexity.

papers_seen.author: Wood
papers_seen.title: What Makes a "Good" Data Augmentation in Knowledge Distillation -- A Statistical Perspective
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a general neural network training approach that uses a teacher model to guide the student model. Existing works mainly study KD from the network output side (e.g., trying to design a better KD loss function), while few have attempted to understand it from the input side. Especially, its interplay with data augmentation (DA) has not been well understood. In this paper, we ask: Why do some DA schemes (e.g., CutMix) inherently perform much better than others in KD? What makes a "good" DA in KD? Our investigation from a statistical perspective suggests that a good DA scheme should reduce the covariance of the teacher-student cross-entropy. A practical metric, the stddev of teacher's mean probability (T. stddev), is further presented and well justified empirically. Besides the theoretical understanding, we also introduce a new entropy-based data-mixing DA scheme, CutMixPick, to further enhance CutMix. Extensive empirical studies support our claims and demonstrate how we can harvest considerable performance gains simply by using a better DA scheme in knowledge distillation.

papers_seen.author: Hernandez
papers_seen.title: R2L: Distilling Neural Radiance Field to Neural Light Field for Efficient Novel View Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Recent research explosion on Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) shows the encouraging potential to represent complex scenes with neural networks. One major drawback of NeRF is its prohibitive inference time: Rendering a single pixel requires querying the NeRF network hundreds of times. To resolve it, existing efforts mainly attempt to reduce the number of required sampled points. However, the problem of iterative sampling still exists. On the other hand, Neural Light Field (NeLF) presents a more straightforward representation over NeRF in novel view synthesis -- the rendering of a pixel amounts to one single forward pass without ray-marching. In this work, we present a deep residual MLP network (88 layers) to effectively learn the light field. We show the key to successfully learning such a deep NeLF network is to have sufficient data, for which we transfer the knowledge from a pre-trained NeRF model via data distillation. Extensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world scenes show the merits of our method over other counterpart algorithms. On the synthetic scenes, we achieve 26-35x FLOPs reduction (per camera ray) and 28-31x runtime speedup, meanwhile delivering significantly better (1.4-2.8 dB average PSNR improvement) rendering quality than NeRF without any customized parallelism requirement.

papers_seen.author: Jackson
papers_seen.title: Online Knowledge Distillation via Mutual Contrastive Learning for Visual Recognition
papers_seen.abstract: The teacher-free online Knowledge Distillation (KD) aims to train an ensemble of multiple student models collaboratively and distill knowledge from each other. Although existing online KD methods achieve desirable performance, they often focus on class probabilities as the core knowledge type, ignoring the valuable feature representational information. We present a Mutual Contrastive Learning (MCL) framework for online KD. The core idea of MCL is to perform mutual interaction and transfer of contrastive distributions among a cohort of networks in an online manner. Our MCL can aggregate cross-network embedding information and maximize the lower bound to the mutual information between two networks. This enables each network to learn extra contrastive knowledge from others, leading to better feature representations, thus improving the performance of visual recognition tasks. Beyond the final layer, we extend MCL to intermediate layers and perform an adaptive layer-matching mechanism trained by meta-optimization. Experiments on image classification and transfer learning to visual recognition tasks show that layer-wise MCL can lead to consistent performance gains against state-of-the-art online KD approaches. The superiority demonstrates that layer-wise MCL can guide the network to generate better feature representations. Our code is publicly avaliable at https://github.com/winycg/L-MCL.

papers_seen.author: Arroyo
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Theory, and Practice
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques have become central to deploying large deep models in resource-constrained settings. Research spans practical recipes (logit matching, feature and layer-wise matching, projector modules), structural compression (architectural transforms, channel/filter reduction), and specialized strategies for NLP models (layer mapping for transformers and task-aware layer selection). Recent work also addresses learning dynamics and theory for wide networks, multi-teacher and meta-learned teaching, and scenarios with limited or no access to original training data. Empirical results show that careful choice of distillation targets, alignment mechanisms, and teacher-student curricula can yield compact models that retain strong performance on downstream tasks while enabling faster inference and smaller memory footprints. Open challenges include task-specific selection of distilled knowledge, robustness and generalization across distributions, and principled guidelines for architecture-aware distillation in transformers.

papers_seen.author: Mckay
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a widely-adopted model compression technique that trains a smaller student model to mimic the behavior of a larger teacher model. This approach enables the deployment of high-performing deep learning models on resource-constrained devices while maintaining competitive accuracy. Knowledge distillation has been applied across multiple domains including computer vision, natural language processing, and speech recognition, with variants adapted to different architectures and specific tasks.

papers_seen.author: Mckay
papers_seen.title: MixKD: Towards Efficient Distillation of Large-scale Language Models
papers_seen.abstract: Large-scale language models have recently demonstrated impressive empirical performance. Nevertheless, the improved results are attained at the price of bigger models, more power consumption, and slower inference, which hinder their applicability to low-resource (both memory and computation) platforms. Knowledge distillation (KD) has been demonstrated as an effective framework for compressing such big models. However, large-scale neural network systems are prone to memorize training instances, and thus tend to make inconsistent predictions when the data distribution is altered slightly. Moreover, the student model has few opportunities to request useful information from the teacher model when there is limited task-specific data available. To address these issues, we propose MixKD, a data-agnostic distillation framework that leverages mixup, a simple yet efficient data augmentation approach, to endow the resulting model with stronger generalization ability. Concretely, in addition to the original training examples, the student model is encouraged to mimic the teacher's behavior on the linear interpolation of example pairs as well. We prove from a theoretical perspective that under reasonable conditions MixKD gives rise to a smaller gap between the generalization error and the empirical error. To verify its effectiveness, we conduct experiments on the GLUE benchmark, where MixKD consistently leads to significant gains over the standard KD training, and outperforms several competitive baselines. Experiments under a limited-data setting and ablation studies further demonstrate the advantages of the proposed approach.

papers_seen.author: Hoffman
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Task-Aware Approach to Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) provides a flexible framework to transfer predictive behavior and internal representations from large, costly models (teachers) to smaller, faster models (students). Across modalities and tasks, KD can both preserve or even improve accuracy while enabling deployment constraints such as lower latency, reduced memory, quantized arithmetic, and multi-task or privacy-aware settings. Realizing these benefits requires matching the distillation strategy to task structure and student capacity: approaches that exploit multi-teacher signals, task-aware layer alignment, teacher adaptation, or self-distillation consistently produce better compressed models. I argue that distillation is not a single recipe but a family of practical, complementary techniques that — when chosen and combined thoughtfully — make state-of-the-art models usable in resource-constrained and application-specific scenarios.

papers_seen.author: Rhodes
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Comprehensive Approach to Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation has emerged as a powerful technique for compressing large neural networks into smaller, more efficient models while maintaining competitive performance. This approach enables the deployment of state-of-the-art deep learning models on resource-constrained devices and accelerates inference times for real-world applications. Through teacher-student learning frameworks, knowledge distillation transfers learned representations from complex models to compact ones, addressing the critical challenge of balancing model capacity with computational efficiency across vision and language tasks.

papers_seen.author: Hicks
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation has emerged as a powerful technique for model compression and knowledge transfer in deep learning and NLP applications. By enabling the transfer of knowledge from large teacher models to smaller, more efficient student models, knowledge distillation addresses critical challenges of inference speed, memory consumption, and computational resource requirements. This approach has been successfully applied across diverse domains including NLP tasks, computer vision, federated learning, and various specialized applications, offering practical solutions for deploying complex models in resource-constrained environments.

papers_seen.author: Robinson
papers_seen.title: Effective Practices and Limits of Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and widely applicable approach to compressing large neural models into smaller, faster, and more deployable students. When combined with complementary strategies—such as pre-training compact architectures, layer-wise or representation-level transfer, task-aware selection of distilled signals, quantization, and federated or data-free techniques—KD can preserve much of teacher performance while meeting resource constraints. However, distillation is not a silver bullet: optimization challenges, mismatch between teacher and student internals, and mismatches between teacher predictions and task needs can limit gains. Careful design choices and evaluation protocols are therefore necessary to obtain robust, privacy-preserving, and task-appropriate compressed models.

papers_seen.author: Osborne
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a widely-adopted technique for training compact and efficient models by transferring knowledge from large teacher models to smaller student models. This approach has become instrumental across diverse domains including computer vision, natural language processing, and specialized applications like graph neural networks and recommender systems. The technique addresses the fundamental challenge of deploying sophisticated deep learning models in resource-constrained environments while maintaining competitive performance levels. Recent advances have expanded the methodology beyond simple output probability matching to include intermediate representations, multi-teacher frameworks, and integration with complementary compression techniques.

papers_seen.author: Valencia
papers_seen.title: Compression of Deep Learning Models for Text: A Survey
papers_seen.abstract: In recent years, the fields of natural language processing (NLP) and information retrieval (IR) have made tremendous progress thanksto deep learning models like Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs), Gated Recurrent Units (GRUs) and Long Short-Term Memory (LSTMs)networks, and Transformer [120] based models like Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT) [24], GenerativePre-training Transformer (GPT-2) [94], Multi-task Deep Neural Network (MT-DNN) [73], Extra-Long Network (XLNet) [134], Text-to-text transfer transformer (T5) [95], T-NLG [98] and GShard [63]. But these models are humongous in size. On the other hand,real world applications demand small model size, low response times and low computational power wattage. In this survey, wediscuss six different types of methods (Pruning, Quantization, Knowledge Distillation, Parameter Sharing, Tensor Decomposition, andSub-quadratic Transformer based methods) for compression of such models to enable their deployment in real industry NLP projects.Given the critical need of building applications with efficient and small models, and the large amount of recently published work inthis area, we believe that this survey organizes the plethora of work done by the 'deep learning for NLP' community in the past fewyears and presents it as a coherent story.

papers_seen.author: Jones
papers_seen.title: Practical Principles for Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and model compression are practical, broadly applicable strategies for deploying large deep models in resource-constrained settings. Across tasks from retrieval and reading comprehension to multimodal generation and federated learning, distillation can preserve much of a teacher model's performance while cutting inference cost, enabling new real-time and on-device applications. Success depends less on a single canonical recipe and more on matching the distillation strategy to the deployment constraints and task: progressive structural compression, task-adaptive architecture search, layer- and feature-aware matching, careful treatment of soft targets and data, and privacy- or communication-aware protocols each address common real-world failure modes. Combining these complementary techniques yields compact students that are both efficient and robust for NLP and other domains.

papers_seen.author: Gardner
papers_seen.title: Adversarially Robust Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is effective for producing small, high-performance neural networks for classification, but these small networks are vulnerable to adversarial attacks. This paper studies how adversarial robustness transfers from teacher to student during knowledge distillation. We find that a large amount of robustness may be inherited by the student even when distilled on only clean images. Second, we introduce Adversarially Robust Distillation (ARD) for distilling robustness onto student networks. In addition to producing small models with high test accuracy like conventional distillation, ARD also passes the superior robustness of large networks onto the student. In our experiments, we find that ARD student models decisively outperform adversarially trained networks of identical architecture in terms of robust accuracy, surpassing state-of-the-art methods on standard robustness benchmarks. Finally, we adapt recent fast adversarial training methods to ARD for accelerated robust distillation.

papers_seen.author: Gardner
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation in Deep Learning: Mechanisms, Challenges, and Applications
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation has emerged as a powerful technique for compressing large neural networks into smaller, more efficient models suitable for deployment in resource-constrained environments. While the method transfers knowledge from a high-capacity teacher network to a smaller student network, recent research reveals significant complexities in how this transfer actually occurs and demonstrates diverse applications across computer vision and natural language processing domains. This paper synthesizes findings on knowledge distillation's effectiveness, identifies key optimization challenges, and explores innovative applications in healthcare, multimodal learning, and federated settings.

papers_seen.author: Rice
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning: A Synthesis of Recent Advances
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and model compression have emerged as essential techniques for deploying large neural networks on resource-constrained devices while maintaining predictive performance. These methods involve transferring knowledge from larger, more complex teacher models to smaller, more efficient student models. This synthesis examines the theoretical foundations, practical applications, and recent innovations in knowledge distillation across computer vision, natural language processing, and specialized domains like object detection and graph neural networks. The review highlights mechanisms that enable successful knowledge transfer, strategies for handling heterogeneous model architectures, data-free distillation approaches, and applications to federated learning and multi-modal learning systems.

papers_seen.author: Perez
papers_seen.title: DINE: Domain Adaptation from Single and Multiple Black-box Predictors
papers_seen.abstract: To ease the burden of labeling, unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) aims to transfer knowledge in previous and related labeled datasets (sources) to a new unlabeled dataset (target). Despite impressive progress, prior methods always need to access the raw source data and develop data-dependent alignment approaches to recognize the target samples in a transductive learning manner, which may raise privacy concerns from source individuals. Several recent studies resort to an alternative solution by exploiting the well-trained white-box model from the source domain, yet, it may still leak the raw data through generative adversarial learning. This paper studies a practical and interesting setting for UDA, where only black-box source models (i.e., only network predictions are available) are provided during adaptation in the target domain. To solve this problem, we propose a new two-step knowledge adaptation framework called DIstill and fine-tuNE (DINE). Taking into consideration the target data structure, DINE first distills the knowledge from the source predictor to a customized target model, then fine-tunes the distilled model to further fit the target domain. Besides, neural networks are not required to be identical across domains in DINE, even allowing effective adaptation on a low-resource device. Empirical results on three UDA scenarios (i.e., single-source, multi-source, and partial-set) confirm that DINE achieves highly competitive performance compared to state-of-the-art data-dependent approaches. Code is available at \url{https://github.com/tim-learn/DINE/}.

papers_seen.author: Lawrence
papers_seen.title: Distilling Knowledge From a Deep Pose Regressor Network
papers_seen.abstract: This paper presents a novel method to distill knowledge from a deep pose regressor network for efficient Visual Odometry (VO). Standard distillation relies on "dark knowledge" for successful knowledge transfer. As this knowledge is not available in pose regression and the teacher prediction is not always accurate, we propose to emphasize the knowledge transfer only when we trust the teacher. We achieve this by using teacher loss as a confidence score which places variable relative importance on the teacher prediction. We inject this confidence score to the main training task via Attentive Imitation Loss (AIL) and when learning the intermediate representation of the teacher through Attentive Hint Training (AHT) approach. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work which successfully distill the knowledge from a deep pose regression network. Our evaluation on the KITTI and Malaga dataset shows that we can keep the student prediction close to the teacher with up to 92.95% parameter reduction and 2.12x faster in computation time.

papers_seen.author: Richards
papers_seen.title: TextKD-GAN: Text Generation using KnowledgeDistillation and Generative Adversarial Networks
papers_seen.abstract: Text generation is of particular interest in many NLP applications such as machine translation, language modeling, and text summarization. Generative adversarial networks (GANs) achieved a remarkable success in high quality image generation in computer vision,and recently, GANs have gained lots of interest from the NLP community as well. However, achieving similar success in NLP would be more challenging due to the discrete nature of text. In this work, we introduce a method using knowledge distillation to effectively exploit GAN setup for text generation. We demonstrate how autoencoders (AEs) can be used for providing a continuous representation of sentences, which is a smooth representation that assign non-zero probabilities to more than one word. We distill this representation to train the generator to synthesize similar smooth representations. We perform a number of experiments to validate our idea using different datasets and show that our proposed approach yields better performance in terms of the BLEU score and Jensen-Shannon distance (JSD) measure compared to traditional GAN-based text generation approaches without pre-training.

papers_seen.author: Walter
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and Natural Language Processing
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a widely-adopted training paradigm that enables the compression of large neural networks by transferring knowledge from a high-capacity teacher model to a more efficient student model. This approach has proven effective across diverse domains including computer vision, natural language processing, speech recognition, and recommendation systems. By leveraging teacher guidance during training, knowledge distillation achieves significant reductions in model size and computational cost while maintaining or even improving student model performance, making it essential for deploying neural networks on resource-constrained devices and enabling practical real-world applications.

papers_seen.author: Gonzalez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Applications, and Open Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses high-capacity models into smaller ones by transferring predictive behavior or internal structure from a teacher to a student. Recent work has expanded KD beyond matching output probabilities to include internal representation matching, flexible layer alignment, multi-teacher training, data-free approaches, and privacy-aware compression. These advances have been applied to NLP (notably BERT compression), vision, graphs, and other domains, while open challenges remain around data heterogeneity, layer alignment, and robust data-free training.

papers_seen.author: Chavez
papers_seen.title: Data-Free Knowledge Distillation for Deep Neural Networks
papers_seen.abstract: Recent advances in model compression have provided procedures for compressing large neural networks to a fraction of their original size while retaining most if not all of their accuracy. However, all of these approaches rely on access to the original training set, which might not always be possible if the network to be compressed was trained on a very large dataset, or on a dataset whose release poses privacy or safety concerns as may be the case for biometrics tasks. We present a method for data-free knowledge distillation, which is able to compress deep neural networks trained on large-scale datasets to a fraction of their size leveraging only some extra metadata to be provided with a pretrained model release. We also explore different kinds of metadata that can be used with our method, and discuss tradeoffs involved in using each of them.

papers_seen.author: Calderon
papers_seen.title: Learning Generalizable Models for Vehicle Routing Problems via Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Recent neural methods for vehicle routing problems always train and test the deep models on the same instance distribution (i.e., uniform). To tackle the consequent cross-distribution generalization concerns, we bring the knowledge distillation to this field and propose an Adaptive Multi-Distribution Knowledge Distillation (AMDKD) scheme for learning more generalizable deep models. Particularly, our AMDKD leverages various knowledge from multiple teachers trained on exemplar distributions to yield a light-weight yet generalist student model. Meanwhile, we equip AMDKD with an adaptive strategy that allows the student to concentrate on difficult distributions, so as to absorb hard-to-master knowledge more effectively. Extensive experimental results show that, compared with the baseline neural methods, our AMDKD is able to achieve competitive results on both unseen in-distribution and out-of-distribution instances, which are either randomly synthesized or adopted from benchmark datasets (i.e., TSPLIB and CVRPLIB). Notably, our AMDKD is generic, and consumes less computational resources for inference.

papers_seen.author: Henderson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation has emerged as a fundamental technique for model compression and knowledge transfer in deep learning and NLP. This approach involves training a lightweight student network to mimic a more powerful teacher network, enabling the creation of efficient models suitable for deployment on resource-constrained devices. The technique has been successfully applied across diverse domains including computer vision, natural language processing, and multimodal learning, addressing the challenge of maintaining high performance while significantly reducing computational requirements and model size.

papers_seen.author: Pacheco
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Powerful Framework for Model Compression and Transfer Learning in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation has emerged as a highly effective approach for compressing large neural networks into smaller, more efficient models while maintaining competitive performance. This technique enables the transfer of knowledge from computationally expensive teacher models to lightweight student networks, making it particularly valuable for deploying models in resource-constrained environments. The method has proven successful across diverse domains including natural language processing, computer vision, and multimodal learning. By leveraging various distillation strategies and loss functions, researchers have demonstrated that knowledge distillation can achieve substantial performance improvements and computational efficiency gains with minimal accuracy loss.

papers_seen.author: Roman
papers_seen.title: Converging Strategies for Practical Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured from a heuristic for compressing classifiers into a versatile, modality-agnostic toolkit that enables deployment of large models in resource-constrained and privacy-sensitive settings. Advances span architectural strategies (progressive module replacement and feature mimicking), data-centric solutions (data-free and augmented distillation), teacher selection (ensembles and meta-learned teachers), and objectives that transfer robustness as well as accuracy. When combined thoughtfully — e.g., targeted feature-level objectives, careful data-generation or augmentation, and teacher optimization — KD enables small models that approach teacher performance while meeting latency, memory, and deployment constraints. This article argues that best practice is not a single KD recipe but an integrated approach that matches the distillation technique to operational constraints (data availability, privacy, robustness requirements, and target hardware).

papers_seen.author: Miller
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation for Improved Accuracy in Spoken Question Answering
papers_seen.abstract: Spoken question answering (SQA) is a challenging task that requires the machine to fully understand the complex spoken documents. Automatic speech recognition (ASR) plays a significant role in the development of QA systems. However, the recent work shows that ASR systems generate highly noisy transcripts, which critically limit the capability of machine comprehension on the SQA task. To address the issue, we present a novel distillation framework. Specifically, we devise a training strategy to perform knowledge distillation (KD) from spoken documents and written counterparts. Our work makes a step towards distilling knowledge from the language model as a supervision signal to lead to better student accuracy by reducing the misalignment between automatic and manual transcriptions. Experiments demonstrate that our approach outperforms several state-of-the-art language models on the Spoken-SQuAD dataset.

papers_seen.author: Garcia
papers_seen.title: Compressing Visual-linguistic Model via Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Despite exciting progress in pre-training for visual-linguistic (VL) representations, very few aspire to a small VL model. In this paper, we study knowledge distillation (KD) to effectively compress a transformer-based large VL model into a small VL model. The major challenge arises from the inconsistent regional visual tokens extracted from different detectors of Teacher and Student, resulting in the misalignment of hidden representations and attention distributions. To address the problem, we retrain and adapt the Teacher by using the same region proposals from Student's detector while the features are from Teacher's own object detector. With aligned network inputs, the adapted Teacher is capable of transferring the knowledge through the intermediate representations. Specifically, we use the mean square error loss to mimic the attention distribution inside the transformer block and present a token-wise noise contrastive loss to align the hidden state by contrasting with negative representations stored in a sample queue. To this end, we show that our proposed distillation significantly improves the performance of small VL models on image captioning and visual question answering tasks. It reaches 120.8 in CIDEr score on COCO captioning, an improvement of 5.1 over its non-distilled counterpart; and an accuracy of 69.8 on VQA 2.0, a 0.8 gain from the baseline. Our extensive experiments and ablations confirm the effectiveness of VL distillation in both pre-training and fine-tuning stages.

papers_seen.author: Clark
papers_seen.title: Collaborative Distillation for Ultra-Resolution Universal Style Transfer
papers_seen.abstract: Universal style transfer methods typically leverage rich representations from deep Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) models (e.g., VGG-19) pre-trained on large collections of images. Despite the effectiveness, its application is heavily constrained by the large model size to handle ultra-resolution images given limited memory. In this work, we present a new knowledge distillation method (named Collaborative Distillation) for encoder-decoder based neural style transfer to reduce the convolutional filters. The main idea is underpinned by a finding that the encoder-decoder pairs construct an exclusive collaborative relationship, which is regarded as a new kind of knowledge for style transfer models. Moreover, to overcome the feature size mismatch when applying collaborative distillation, a linear embedding loss is introduced to drive the student network to learn a linear embedding of the teacher's features. Extensive experiments show the effectiveness of our method when applied to different universal style transfer approaches (WCT and AdaIN), even if the model size is reduced by 15.5 times. Especially, on WCT with the compressed models, we achieve ultra-resolution (over 40 megapixels) universal style transfer on a 12GB GPU for the first time. Further experiments on optimization-based stylization scheme show the generality of our algorithm on different stylization paradigms. Our code and trained models are available at https://github.com/mingsun-tse/collaborative-distillation.

papers_seen.author: Zuniga
papers_seen.title: Large scale distributed neural network training through online distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Techniques such as ensembling and distillation promise model quality improvements when paired with almost any base model. However, due to increased test-time cost (for ensembles) and increased complexity of the training pipeline (for distillation), these techniques are challenging to use in industrial settings. In this paper we explore a variant of distillation which is relatively straightforward to use as it does not require a complicated multi-stage setup or many new hyperparameters. Our first claim is that online distillation enables us to use extra parallelism to fit very large datasets about twice as fast. Crucially, we can still speed up training even after we have already reached the point at which additional parallelism provides no benefit for synchronous or asynchronous stochastic gradient descent. Two neural networks trained on disjoint subsets of the data can share knowledge by encouraging each model to agree with the predictions the other model would have made. These predictions can come from a stale version of the other model so they can be safely computed using weights that only rarely get transmitted. Our second claim is that online distillation is a cost-effective way to make the exact predictions of a model dramatically more reproducible. We support our claims using experiments on the Criteo Display Ad Challenge dataset, ImageNet, and the largest to-date dataset used for neural language modeling, containing $6\times 10^{11}$ tokens and based on the Common Crawl repository of web data.

Experiments under a limited-data setting and ablation studies further demonstrate the advantages of the proposed approach."}, {'author': 'Hoffman', 'year': 2021, 'title': 'Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Task-Aware Approach to Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP', 'abstract': 'Knowledge distillation (KD) provides a flexible framework to transfer predictive behavior and internal representations from large, costly models (teachers) to smaller, faster models (students). In this work, we present a new knowledge distillation method (named Collaborative Distillation) for encoder-decoder based neural style transfer to reduce the convolutional filters. The main idea is underpinned by a finding that the encoder-decoder pairs construct an exclusive collaborative relationship, which is regarded as a new kind of knowledge for style transfer models.
