papers_seen.author: Wright
papers_seen.title: Distilled Semantics for Comprehensive Scene Understanding from Videos
papers_seen.abstract: Whole understanding of the surroundings is paramount to autonomous systems. Recent works have shown that deep neural networks can learn geometry (depth) and motion (optical flow) from a monocular video without any explicit supervision from ground truth annotations, particularly hard to source for these two tasks. In this paper, we take an additional step toward holistic scene understanding with monocular cameras by learning depth and motion alongside with semantics, with supervision for the latter provided by a pre-trained network distilling proxy ground truth images. We address the three tasks jointly by a) a novel training protocol based on knowledge distillation and self-supervision and b) a compact network architecture which enables efficient scene understanding on both power hungry GPUs and low-power embedded platforms. We thoroughly assess the performance of our framework and show that it yields state-of-the-art results for monocular depth estimation, optical flow and motion segmentation.

papers_seen.author: Hill
papers_seen.title: A Deep Hierarchical Approach to Lifelong Learning in Minecraft
papers_seen.abstract: We propose a lifelong learning system that has the ability to reuse and transfer knowledge from one task to another while efficiently retaining the previously learned knowledge-base. Knowledge is transferred by learning reusable skills to solve tasks in Minecraft, a popular video game which is an unsolved and high-dimensional lifelong learning problem. These reusable skills, which we refer to as Deep Skill Networks, are then incorporated into our novel Hierarchical Deep Reinforcement Learning Network (H-DRLN) architecture using two techniques: (1) a deep skill array and (2) skill distillation, our novel variation of policy distillation (Rusu et. al. 2015) for learning skills. Skill distillation enables the HDRLN to efficiently retain knowledge and therefore scale in lifelong learning, by accumulating knowledge and encapsulating multiple reusable skills into a single distilled network. The H-DRLN exhibits superior performance and lower learning sample complexity compared to the regular Deep Q Network (Mnih et. al. 2015) in sub-domains of Minecraft.

papers_seen.author: Williams
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Techniques in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques have become central tools for shrinking large neural networks while retaining much of their predictive performance. Researchers have adapted KD beyond classification to tasks such as object detection, generative modeling, machine translation, and sequence-to-sequence systems, and have explored many variants including feature imitation, teacher ensembles, sample selection, communication-efficient distributed protocols, and robustness-aware distillation. Empirical work shows KD can yield substantial savings in parameter count, memory, and runtime while often preserving accuracy; however, task-specific challenges, teacher-student mismatches, and distributional or adversarial vulnerabilities require modified objectives, architectures, or training curricula to transfer the right form of “dark” knowledge. The field is moving toward methods that (a) shape teacher outputs or training so distilled information is student-friendly, (b) target intermediate features and decision boundaries rather than only logits, and (c) adapt to resource- and privacy-constrained settings such as federated or few-shot compression.

papers_seen.author: Evans
papers_seen.title: Learning Compact Metrics for MT
papers_seen.abstract: Recent developments in machine translation and multilingual text generation have led researchers to adopt trained metrics such as COMET or BLEURT, which treat evaluation as a regression problem and use representations from multilingual pre-trained models such as XLM-RoBERTa or mBERT. Yet studies on related tasks suggest that these models are most efficient when they are large, which is costly and impractical for evaluation. We investigate the trade-off between multilinguality and model capacity with RemBERT, a state-of-the-art multilingual language model, using data from the WMT Metrics Shared Task. We present a series of experiments which show that model size is indeed a bottleneck for cross-lingual transfer, then demonstrate how distillation can help addressing this bottleneck, by leveraging synthetic data generation and transferring knowledge from one teacher to multiple students trained on related languages. Our method yields up to 10.5% improvement over vanilla fine-tuning and reaches 92.6% of RemBERT's performance using only a third of its parameters.

papers_seen.author: Valencia
papers_seen.title: Beyond Soft Labels: A Multi-Objective View of Knowledge Distillation for Robust, Efficient Models
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a practical route to compress large neural models for deployment, but treating distillation as merely matching teacher output probabilities limits what can be transferred and how reliably the student will generalize. This paper argues that effective distillation should combine representation-level transfer, channel- and feature-aware objectives, confidence-weighted multi-teacher signals, domain adaptation, and training-time efficiency techniques, while explicitly attending to optimization gaps and fairness concerns. We synthesize evidence across methods and propose a prioritized, pragmatic pipeline for producing compact models that better retain teacher knowledge, scale in production, and reduce unintended harms.

papers_seen.author: Ellis
papers_seen.title: On Representation Knowledge Distillation for Graph Neural Networks
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a learning paradigm for boosting resource-efficient graph neural networks (GNNs) using more expressive yet cumbersome teacher models. Past work on distillation for GNNs proposed the Local Structure Preserving loss (LSP), which matches local structural relationships defined over edges across the student and teacher's node embeddings. This paper studies whether preserving the global topology of how the teacher embeds graph data can be a more effective distillation objective for GNNs, as real-world graphs often contain latent interactions and noisy edges. We propose Graph Contrastive Representation Distillation (G-CRD), which uses contrastive learning to implicitly preserve global topology by aligning the student node embeddings to those of the teacher in a shared representation space. Additionally, we introduce an expanded set of benchmarks on large-scale real-world datasets where the performance gap between teacher and student GNNs is non-negligible. Experiments across 4 datasets and 14 heterogeneous GNN architectures show that G-CRD consistently boosts the performance and robustness of lightweight GNNs, outperforming LSP (and a global structure preserving variant of LSP) as well as baselines from 2D computer vision. An analysis of the representational similarity among teacher and student embedding spaces reveals that G-CRD balances preserving local and global relationships, while structure preserving approaches are best at preserving one or the other. Our code is available at https://github.com/chaitjo/efficient-gnns

papers_seen.author: Ray
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a fundamental technique for model compression that enables the transfer of knowledge from large, complex neural networks (teacher models) to smaller, more efficient student models. This approach has proven effective across diverse domains including computer vision, natural language processing, and recommendation systems. The technique works by training a lightweight student model to replicate the behavior of a more powerful teacher model, typically using soft probability targets rather than hard labels. Knowledge distillation addresses the critical challenge of deploying deep neural networks in resource-constrained environments while maintaining performance, making it highly relevant for real-world applications requiring low latency and computational efficiency.

papers_seen.author: Bowman
papers_seen.title: TRILLsson: Distilled Universal Paralinguistic Speech Representations
papers_seen.abstract: Recent advances in self-supervision have dramatically improved the quality of speech representations. However, deployment of state-of-the-art embedding models on devices has been restricted due to their limited public availability and large resource footprint. Our work addresses these issues by publicly releasing a collection of paralinguistic speech models that are small and near state-of-the-art performance. Our approach is based on knowledge distillation, and our models are distilled on public data only. We explore different architectures and thoroughly evaluate our models on the Non-Semantic Speech (NOSS) benchmark. Our largest distilled model is less than 15% the size of the original model (314MB vs 2.2GB), achieves over 96% the accuracy on 6 of 7 tasks, and is trained on 6.5% the data. The smallest model is 1% in size (22MB) and achieves over 90% the accuracy on 6 of 7 tasks. Our models outperform the open source Wav2Vec 2.0 model on 6 of 7 tasks, and our smallest model outperforms the open source Wav2Vec 2.0 on both emotion recognition tasks despite being 7% the size.

papers_seen.author: Maddox
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core Strategy for Compression, Regularization and Privacy-Preserving Transfer
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and flexible approach for compressing high-capacity models into lightweight students while preserving or even improving generalization. Beyond simple teacher–student logits matching, KD can transfer architectural inductive biases, act as an effective regularizer, enable compression without access to original training data, and be adapted to low-data and multi-teacher settings. The choice of distillation objective, the availability of data, and the reliability of teacher signals determine success; consequently, a portfolio of techniques (data synthesis, augmentation, calibrated divergences, and confidence-aware aggregation) is needed to make KD robust and widely applicable in deep learning and NLP deployments.

papers_seen.author: Johnson
papers_seen.title: Mitigating Gender Bias in Distilled Language Models via Counterfactual Role Reversal
papers_seen.abstract: Language models excel at generating coherent text, and model compression techniques such as knowledge distillation have enabled their use in resource-constrained settings. However, these models can be biased in multiple ways, including the unfounded association of male and female genders with gender-neutral professions. Therefore, knowledge distillation without any fairness constraints may preserve or exaggerate the teacher model's biases onto the distilled model. To this end, we present a novel approach to mitigate gender disparity in text generation by learning a fair model during knowledge distillation. We propose two modifications to the base knowledge distillation based on counterfactual role reversal$\unicode{x2014}$modifying teacher probabilities and augmenting the training set. We evaluate gender polarity across professions in open-ended text generated from the resulting distilled and finetuned GPT$\unicode{x2012}$2 models and demonstrate a substantial reduction in gender disparity with only a minor compromise in utility. Finally, we observe that language models that reduce gender polarity in language generation do not improve embedding fairness or downstream classification fairness.

papers_seen.author: Rogers
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression: Essential Techniques for Deploying Deep Learning Models
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and model compression have emerged as critical techniques for enabling the deployment of large, powerful deep learning models in resource-constrained environments. By transferring knowledge from larger teacher models to smaller student models, these methods address the fundamental challenge of making state-of-the-art models practical for real-world applications that require fast inference and limited computational resources.

papers_seen.author: Valencia
papers_seen.title: Compression of Deep Learning Models for Text: A Survey
papers_seen.abstract: In recent years, the fields of natural language processing (NLP) and information retrieval (IR) have made tremendous progress thanksto deep learning models like Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs), Gated Recurrent Units (GRUs) and Long Short-Term Memory (LSTMs)networks, and Transformer [120] based models like Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT) [24], GenerativePre-training Transformer (GPT-2) [94], Multi-task Deep Neural Network (MT-DNN) [73], Extra-Long Network (XLNet) [134], Text-to-text transfer transformer (T5) [95], T-NLG [98] and GShard [63]. But these models are humongous in size. On the other hand,real world applications demand small model size, low response times and low computational power wattage. In this survey, wediscuss six different types of methods (Pruning, Quantization, Knowledge Distillation, Parameter Sharing, Tensor Decomposition, andSub-quadratic Transformer based methods) for compression of such models to enable their deployment in real industry NLP projects.Given the critical need of building applications with efficient and small models, and the large amount of recently published work inthis area, we believe that this survey organizes the plethora of work done by the 'deep learning for NLP' community in the past fewyears and presents it as a coherent story.

papers_seen.author: Wood
papers_seen.title: What Makes a "Good" Data Augmentation in Knowledge Distillation -- A Statistical Perspective
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a general neural network training approach that uses a teacher model to guide the student model. Existing works mainly study KD from the network output side (e.g., trying to design a better KD loss function), while few have attempted to understand it from the input side. Especially, its interplay with data augmentation (DA) has not been well understood. In this paper, we ask: Why do some DA schemes (e.g., CutMix) inherently perform much better than others in KD? What makes a "good" DA in KD? Our investigation from a statistical perspective suggests that a good DA scheme should reduce the covariance of the teacher-student cross-entropy. A practical metric, the stddev of teacher's mean probability (T. stddev), is further presented and well justified empirically. Besides the theoretical understanding, we also introduce a new entropy-based data-mixing DA scheme, CutMixPick, to further enhance CutMix. Extensive empirical studies support our claims and demonstrate how we can harvest considerable performance gains simply by using a better DA scheme in knowledge distillation.

papers_seen.author: Liu
papers_seen.title: Enabling Multimodal Generation on CLIP via Vision-Language Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: The recent large-scale vision-language pre-training (VLP) of dual-stream architectures (e.g., CLIP) with a tremendous amount of image-text pair data, has shown its superiority on various multimodal alignment tasks. Despite its success, the resulting models are not capable of multimodal generative tasks due to the weak text encoder. To tackle this problem, we propose to augment the dual-stream VLP model with a textual pre-trained language model (PLM) via vision-language knowledge distillation (VLKD), enabling the capability for multimodal generation. VLKD is pretty data- and computation-efficient compared to the pre-training from scratch. Experimental results show that the resulting model has strong zero-shot performance on multimodal generation tasks, such as open-ended visual question answering and image captioning. For example, it achieves 44.5% zero-shot accuracy on the VQAv2 dataset, surpassing the previous state-of-the-art zero-shot model with $7\times$ fewer parameters. Furthermore, the original textual language understanding and generation ability of the PLM is maintained after VLKD, which makes our model versatile for both multimodal and unimodal tasks.

papers_seen.author: Nguyen
papers_seen.title: The Central Role of Knowledge Distillation for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a practical, versatile approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, faster, and more deployable students. Across modalities and architectures, distillation enables substantial reductions in memory and compute while retaining most of the teacher performance; it also supports privacy-preserving deployment, task-adaptive compression, and specialized objectives (e.g., generation, graph learning, or speech). However, the effectiveness of distillation depends on careful design choices—teacher selection or synthesis, optimization and data regimes, and complementary strategies such as multi-teacher schemes or architecture search. When combined with privacy or architecture-aware methods, distillation becomes an essential tool for bringing state-of-the-art models into practical systems.

papers_seen.author: Abbott
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Methods in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression techniques have become central to deploying high-performing deep models under computational, memory, privacy, and latency constraints. Work in this area spans traditional teacher→student soft-target distillation, distillation of internal representations, data-free or zero-shot approaches for when training data are unavailable, online and mutual distillation among peers, multi-teacher and ensemble-based strategies, and adaptations for domain shifts and task-specific requirements (e.g., non-autoregressive translation). Empirical findings emphasize that distillation often reduces training data complexity and transfers information most effectively when methods account for representation mismatch, data generation or augmentation, teacher–student capacity differences, and the distributional specifics of the task. Practical trends favor hybrid pipelines that combine soft-targets with representation matching, selective use of raw or synthesized data, and scalable online/ensemble procedures to support large datasets and heterogeneous deployment scenarios.

papers_seen.author: Fowler
papers_seen.title: SEED: Self-supervised Distillation For Visual Representation
papers_seen.abstract: This paper is concerned with self-supervised learning for small models. The problem is motivated by our empirical studies that while the widely used contrastive self-supervised learning method has shown great progress on large model training, it does not work well for small models. To address this problem, we propose a new learning paradigm, named SElf-SupErvised Distillation (SEED), where we leverage a larger network (as Teacher) to transfer its representational knowledge into a smaller architecture (as Student) in a self-supervised fashion. Instead of directly learning from unlabeled data, we train a student encoder to mimic the similarity score distribution inferred by a teacher over a set of instances. We show that SEED dramatically boosts the performance of small networks on downstream tasks. Compared with self-supervised baselines, SEED improves the top-1 accuracy from 42.2% to 67.6% on EfficientNet-B0 and from 36.3% to 68.2% on MobileNet-v3-Large on the ImageNet-1k dataset.

papers_seen.author: Rodriguez
papers_seen.title: Releasing Graph Neural Networks with Differential Privacy Guarantees
papers_seen.abstract: With the increasing popularity of graph neural networks (GNNs) in several sensitive applications like healthcare and medicine, concerns have been raised over the privacy aspects of trained GNNs. More notably, GNNs are vulnerable to privacy attacks, such as membership inference attacks, even if only black-box access to the trained model is granted. We propose PrivGNN, a privacy-preserving framework for releasing GNN models in a centralized setting. Assuming an access to a public unlabeled graph, PrivGNN provides a framework to release GNN models trained explicitly on public data along with knowledge obtained from the private data in a privacy preserving manner. PrivGNN combines the knowledge-distillation framework with the two noise mechanisms, random subsampling, and noisy labeling, to ensure rigorous privacy guarantees. We theoretically analyze our approach in the Renyi differential privacy framework. Besides, we show the solid experimental performance of our method compared to several baselines adapted for graph-structured data. Our code is available at https://github.com/iyempissy/privGnn.

papers_seen.author: Parsons
papers_seen.title: Curriculum Learning for Dense Retrieval Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Recent work has shown that more effective dense retrieval models can be obtained by distilling ranking knowledge from an existing base re-ranking model. In this paper, we propose a generic curriculum learning based optimization framework called CL-DRD that controls the difficulty level of training data produced by the re-ranking (teacher) model. CL-DRD iteratively optimizes the dense retrieval (student) model by increasing the difficulty of the knowledge distillation data made available to it. In more detail, we initially provide the student model coarse-grained preference pairs between documents in the teacher's ranking and progressively move towards finer-grained pairwise document ordering requirements. In our experiments, we apply a simple implementation of the CL-DRD framework to enhance two state-of-the-art dense retrieval models. Experiments on three public passage retrieval datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed framework.

papers_seen.author: Roberts
papers_seen.title: Improving the Interpretability of Deep Neural Networks with Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Deep Neural Networks have achieved huge success at a wide spectrum of applications from language modeling, computer vision to speech recognition. However, nowadays, good performance alone is not sufficient to satisfy the needs of practical deployment where interpretability is demanded for cases involving ethics and mission critical applications. The complex models of Deep Neural Networks make it hard to understand and reason the predictions, which hinders its further progress. To tackle this problem, we apply the Knowledge Distillation technique to distill Deep Neural Networks into decision trees in order to attain good performance and interpretability simultaneously. We formulate the problem at hand as a multi-output regression problem and the experiments demonstrate that the student model achieves significantly better accuracy performance (about 1\% to 5\%) than vanilla decision trees at the same level of tree depth. The experiments are implemented on the TensorFlow platform to make it scalable to big datasets. To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to distill Deep Neural Networks into vanilla decision trees on multi-class datasets.

papers_seen.author: Rios
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a technique for transferring knowledge from a large, complex teacher model to a smaller, more efficient student model. This approach enables model compression while maintaining performance, making it valuable for deployment on resource-constrained devices. Knowledge distillation has been successfully applied across various domains including computer vision, natural language processing, speech recognition, and federated learning, addressing both computational efficiency and interpretability challenges in deep neural networks.

papers_seen.author: Wright
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and Natural Language Processing
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a powerful technique for model compression and knowledge transfer in deep learning, enabling the training of smaller, more efficient student models to mimic the behavior of larger teacher models. This approach has become increasingly important for deploying neural networks on resource-constrained devices while maintaining competitive accuracy. The technique has been extensively studied across diverse domains including natural language processing, computer vision, federated learning, and generative models, with various architectural innovations and theoretical frameworks developed to improve its effectiveness and applicability.

papers_seen.author: Lynch
papers_seen.title: The Case for Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Multifaceted Tool for Model Compression and Transfer
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation has matured from a single-purpose compression trick into a flexible framework that can compress models, transfer inductive biases, improve fairness and domain adaptability, and support continual learning across modalities. Its strengths come from multiple instantiations—logit matching, feature mimicking, contrastive representation alignment, module replacement, and automated search guided by distillation—which together make it broadly applicable for deploying high-performing models under resource constraints. At the same time, careful choice of distillation targets, mixture with hard labels, and awareness of teacher imperfections are key to realizing its benefits in practice.

papers_seen.author: Herrera
papers_seen.title: Compressing GANs using Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) have been used in several machine learning tasks such as domain transfer, super resolution, and synthetic data generation. State-of-the-art GANs often use tens of millions of parameters, making them expensive to deploy for applications in low SWAP (size, weight, and power) hardware, such as mobile devices, and for applications with real time capabilities. There has been no work found to reduce the number of parameters used in GANs. Therefore, we propose a method to compress GANs using knowledge distillation techniques, in which a smaller "student" GAN learns to mimic a larger "teacher" GAN. We show that the distillation methods used on MNIST, CIFAR-10, and Celeb-A datasets can compress teacher GANs at ratios of 1669:1, 58:1, and 87:1, respectively, while retaining the quality of the generated image. From our experiments, we observe a qualitative limit for GAN's compression. Moreover, we observe that, with a fixed parameter budget, compressed GANs outperform GANs trained using standard training methods. We conjecture that this is partially owing to the optimization landscape of over-parameterized GANs which allows efficient training using alternating gradient descent. Thus, training an over-parameterized GAN followed by our proposed compression scheme provides a high quality generative model with a small number of parameters.

papers_seen.author: Baker
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a model compression technique that transfers knowledge from large, high-capacity "teacher" networks to smaller, efficient "student" networks. This approach enables the deployment of deep learning models in resource-constrained environments while maintaining competitive performance. Knowledge distillation has been successfully applied across diverse domains including computer vision, natural language processing, speech recognition, and specialized applications such as recommendation systems and reinforcement learning. The technique addresses critical challenges in practical deployment by reducing computational costs, memory footprint, and inference latency.

papers_seen.author: Smith
papers_seen.title: AutoGAN-Distiller: Searching to Compress Generative Adversarial Networks
papers_seen.abstract: The compression of Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) has lately drawn attention, due to the increasing demand for deploying GANs into mobile devices for numerous applications such as image translation, enhancement and editing. However, compared to the substantial efforts to compressing other deep models, the research on compressing GANs (usually the generators) remains at its infancy stage. Existing GAN compression algorithms are limited to handling specific GAN architectures and losses. Inspired by the recent success of AutoML in deep compression, we introduce AutoML to GAN compression and develop an AutoGAN-Distiller (AGD) framework. Starting with a specifically designed efficient search space, AGD performs an end-to-end discovery for new efficient generators, given the target computational resource constraints. The search is guided by the original GAN model via knowledge distillation, therefore fulfilling the compression. AGD is fully automatic, standalone (i.e., needing no trained discriminators), and generically applicable to various GAN models. We evaluate AGD in two representative GAN tasks: image translation and super resolution. Without bells and whistles, AGD yields remarkably lightweight yet more competitive compressed models, that largely outperform existing alternatives. Our codes and pretrained models are available at https://github.com/TAMU-VITA/AGD.

papers_seen.author: Martin
papers_seen.title: Distilling the Knowledge of BERT for Sequence-to-Sequence ASR
papers_seen.abstract: Attention-based sequence-to-sequence (seq2seq) models have achieved promising results in automatic speech recognition (ASR). However, as these models decode in a left-to-right way, they do not have access to context on the right. We leverage both left and right context by applying BERT as an external language model to seq2seq ASR through knowledge distillation. In our proposed method, BERT generates soft labels to guide the training of seq2seq ASR. Furthermore, we leverage context beyond the current utterance as input to BERT. Experimental evaluations show that our method significantly improves the ASR performance from the seq2seq baseline on the Corpus of Spontaneous Japanese (CSJ). Knowledge distillation from BERT outperforms that from a transformer LM that only looks at left context. We also show the effectiveness of leveraging context beyond the current utterance. Our method outperforms other LM application approaches such as n-best rescoring and shallow fusion, while it does not require extra inference cost.

papers_seen.author: Clark
papers_seen.title: Towards Model Agnostic Federated Learning Using Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Is it possible to design an universal API for federated learning using which an ad-hoc group of data-holders (agents) collaborate with each other and perform federated learning? Such an API would necessarily need to be model-agnostic i.e. make no assumption about the model architecture being used by the agents, and also cannot rely on having representative public data at hand. Knowledge distillation (KD) is the obvious tool of choice to design such protocols. However, surprisingly, we show that most natural KD-based federated learning protocols have poor performance.   To investigate this, we propose a new theoretical framework, Federated Kernel ridge regression, which can capture both model heterogeneity as well as data heterogeneity. Our analysis shows that the degradation is largely due to a fundamental limitation of knowledge distillation under data heterogeneity. We further validate our framework by analyzing and designing new protocols based on KD. Their performance on real world experiments using neural networks, though still unsatisfactory, closely matches our theoretical predictions.

papers_seen.author: Wolfe
papers_seen.title: Robust and Resource-Efficient Data-Free Knowledge Distillation by Generative Pseudo Replay
papers_seen.abstract: Data-Free Knowledge Distillation (KD) allows knowledge transfer from a trained neural network (teacher) to a more compact one (student) in the absence of original training data. Existing works use a validation set to monitor the accuracy of the student over real data and report the highest performance throughout the entire process. However, validation data may not be available at distillation time either, making it infeasible to record the student snapshot that achieved the peak accuracy. Therefore, a practical data-free KD method should be robust and ideally provide monotonically increasing student accuracy during distillation. This is challenging because the student experiences knowledge degradation due to the distribution shift of the synthetic data. A straightforward approach to overcome this issue is to store and rehearse the generated samples periodically, which increases the memory footprint and creates privacy concerns. We propose to model the distribution of the previously observed synthetic samples with a generative network. In particular, we design a Variational Autoencoder (VAE) with a training objective that is customized to learn the synthetic data representations optimally. The student is rehearsed by the generative pseudo replay technique, with samples produced by the VAE. Hence knowledge degradation can be prevented without storing any samples. Experiments on image classification benchmarks show that our method optimizes the expected value of the distilled model accuracy while eliminating the large memory overhead incurred by the sample-storing methods.

papers_seen.author: Gaines
papers_seen.title: AdaBERT: Task-Adaptive BERT Compression with Differentiable Neural Architecture Search
papers_seen.abstract: Large pre-trained language models such as BERT have shown their effectiveness in various natural language processing tasks. However, the huge parameter size makes them difficult to be deployed in real-time applications that require quick inference with limited resources. Existing methods compress BERT into small models while such compression is task-independent, i.e., the same compressed BERT for all different downstream tasks. Motivated by the necessity and benefits of task-oriented BERT compression, we propose a novel compression method, AdaBERT, that leverages differentiable Neural Architecture Search to automatically compress BERT into task-adaptive small models for specific tasks. We incorporate a task-oriented knowledge distillation loss to provide search hints and an efficiency-aware loss as search constraints, which enables a good trade-off between efficiency and effectiveness for task-adaptive BERT compression. We evaluate AdaBERT on several NLP tasks, and the results demonstrate that those task-adaptive compressed models are 12.7x to 29.3x faster than BERT in inference time and 11.5x to 17.0x smaller in terms of parameter size, while comparable performance is maintained.

papers_seen.author: Robinson
papers_seen.title: Effective Practices and Limits of Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and widely applicable approach to compressing large neural models into smaller, faster, and more deployable students. When combined with complementary strategies—such as pre-training compact architectures, layer-wise or representation-level transfer, task-aware selection of distilled signals, quantization, and federated or data-free techniques—KD can preserve much of teacher performance while meeting resource constraints. However, distillation is not a silver bullet: optimization challenges, mismatch between teacher and student internals, and mismatches between teacher predictions and task needs can limit gains. Careful design choices and evaluation protocols are therefore necessary to obtain robust, privacy-preserving, and task-appropriate compressed models.

papers_seen.author: Davis
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Practical Keystone for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practically essential family of techniques for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable ones without sacrificing much task performance. Across supervised, self-supervised, federated, and data-constrained settings, KD enables latency- and memory-efficient deployment, supports domain adaptation, and can be adapted to privacy-sensitive and distributed workflows. Advances in KD emphasize not only learning from teacher logits but also mimicking intermediate features, designing student-friendly teacher objectives, and automating student architectures for specific tasks—yielding a spectrum of methods that together make model compression tractable in real-world NLP and vision systems.

papers_seen.author: Valencia
papers_seen.title: Beyond Soft Labels: A Multi-Objective View of Knowledge Distillation for Robust, Efficient Models
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a practical route to compress large neural models for deployment, but treating distillation as merely matching teacher output probabilities limits what can be transferred and how reliably the student will generalize. This paper argues that effective distillation should combine representation-level transfer, channel- and feature-aware objectives, confidence-weighted multi-teacher signals, domain adaptation, and training-time efficiency techniques, while explicitly attending to optimization gaps and fairness concerns. We synthesize evidence across methods and propose a prioritized, pragmatic pipeline for producing compact models that better retain teacher knowledge, scale in production, and reduce unintended harms.

papers_seen.author: Humphrey
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression: Essential Techniques for Deploying Deep Learning Models in Practice
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation has emerged as a powerful and versatile technique for compressing deep neural networks and improving their practical deployability. By enabling smaller "student" networks to learn from larger "teacher" models, knowledge distillation addresses critical challenges in deploying deep learning systems across diverse domains and hardware constraints. This approach achieves significant model compression ratios while maintaining or even improving performance, making it invaluable for applications requiring efficient inference, interpretability, and resource-constrained deployment. The technique extends beyond simple model compression to encompass diverse applications including natural language processing, computer vision, reinforcement learning, and federated learning, demonstrating its fundamental importance in modern machine learning practice.

papers_seen.author: Miller
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Techniques in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related model compression techniques have matured into a diverse set of theoretical and practical approaches for producing smaller, faster, or more specialized models from larger ones. Work in this area ranges from formal analyses of when and why distillation helps, to engineering advances that reduce runtime cost, enable training without original data, transfer across modalities, improve robustness and privacy, and tailor distilled models for downstream tasks or heterogeneous deployment environments. Practical methods include mimicking logits, matching intermediate representations or attention, progressively replacing modules, using student-focused filtering of teacher signals, and leveraging data augmentation or online collaboration between models. Emerging directions emphasize theoretical understanding, task-aware selection of distilled information, privacy-preserving or data-free pipelines, and retaining adversarial robustness while reducing model size.

papers_seen.author: Adams
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Vital Strategy for Efficient Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation has emerged as a powerful and versatile technique for model compression and efficient deployment of deep neural networks. By transferring knowledge from larger, well-trained teacher models to compact student networks, this approach enables significant reductions in computational requirements while maintaining or even improving performance. This paper argues that knowledge distillation is indispensable for modern machine learning applications, particularly in NLP and computer vision, where the trade-off between model complexity and efficiency remains critical for real-world deployment.

papers_seen.author: Stewart
papers_seen.title: The Case for Knowledge Distillation as a Core Tool for Model Compression Across Modalities
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a flexible, domain-agnostic strategy that enables deployment of high-performing deep models in resource-constrained settings. By transferring predictive behavior, intermediate representations, or distilled data between teacher and student, KD supports compression of generators, discriminative models, and multimodal systems, while enabling privacy-preserving and data-free workflows. When combined with careful pre-training, many-to-many layer alignment, or generative replay, KD allows compact architectures to approach the performance of large teachers and, in some cases, inherit desirable properties such as robustness or interpretability. This paper argues that KD should be treated as a foundational method in model compression toolkits and proposes practical emphases for future work: preserving internal representations, supporting data-free distillation, leveraging pre-training for small models, and distilling robustness.

papers_seen.author: Perez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and Natural Language Processing
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a widely-adopted technique for compressing neural networks by transferring knowledge from a larger teacher model to a smaller student model. This approach enables the development of efficient models with reduced parameters and computational requirements while maintaining high performance across various domains including computer vision and natural language processing. The field has evolved to encompass diverse methodologies, from basic logit matching to advanced layer-wise and feature-level distillation approaches, with applications spanning machine translation, question answering, sentiment analysis, and multi-modal learning.

papers_seen.author: Walter
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation from A Stronger Teacher
papers_seen.abstract: Unlike existing knowledge distillation methods focus on the baseline settings, where the teacher models and training strategies are not that strong and competing as state-of-the-art approaches, this paper presents a method dubbed DIST to distill better from a stronger teacher. We empirically find that the discrepancy of predictions between the student and a stronger teacher may tend to be fairly severer. As a result, the exact match of predictions in KL divergence would disturb the training and make existing methods perform poorly. In this paper, we show that simply preserving the relations between the predictions of teacher and student would suffice, and propose a correlation-based loss to capture the intrinsic inter-class relations from the teacher explicitly. Besides, considering that different instances have different semantic similarities to each class, we also extend this relational match to the intra-class level. Our method is simple yet practical, and extensive experiments demonstrate that it adapts well to various architectures, model sizes and training strategies, and can achieve state-of-the-art performance consistently on image classification, object detection, and semantic segmentation tasks. Code is available at: https://github.com/hunto/DIST_KD .

papers_seen.author: Foster
papers_seen.title: Ensemble Knowledge Distillation for CTR Prediction
papers_seen.abstract: Recently, deep learning-based models have been widely studied for click-through rate (CTR) prediction and lead to improved prediction accuracy in many industrial applications. However, current research focuses primarily on building complex network architectures to better capture sophisticated feature interactions and dynamic user behaviors. The increased model complexity may slow down online inference and hinder its adoption in real-time applications. Instead, our work targets at a new model training strategy based on knowledge distillation (KD). KD is a teacher-student learning framework to transfer knowledge learned from a teacher model to a student model. The KD strategy not only allows us to simplify the student model as a vanilla DNN model but also achieves significant accuracy improvements over the state-of-the-art teacher models. The benefits thus motivate us to further explore the use of a powerful ensemble of teachers for more accurate student model training. We also propose some novel techniques to facilitate ensembled CTR prediction, including teacher gating and early stopping by distillation loss. We conduct comprehensive experiments against 12 existing models and across three industrial datasets. Both offline and online A/B testing results show the effectiveness of our KD-based training strategy.

papers_seen.author: Jackson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning: Methods, Applications, and Empirical Insights
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a widely adopted technique for compressing large neural networks into smaller, more efficient models by transferring knowledge from a teacher network to a student network. This approach has become increasingly important for deploying deep learning models in resource-constrained environments such as mobile and edge devices. The field encompasses diverse methodologies ranging from feature-level distillation to cross-modal approaches, with applications spanning computer vision, natural language processing, and multimodal learning. Recent research has advanced both theoretical understanding and practical implementations of knowledge distillation, demonstrating significant improvements in model compression while maintaining predictive performance.

papers_seen.author: Hurst
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Practices in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques have matured into a diverse set of methods for producing smaller, faster, and sometimes more robust models from larger teachers. Approaches span from soft-label and internal-representation transfer to data-free distillation, federated/distilled training for privacy and communication efficiency, and task-adaptive architecture search for large pretrained language models. Empirical work shows KD can improve inference efficiency with limited accuracy loss, transfer adversarial robustness, and enable effective low-precision and task-specific compressed models, while theoretical analyses and algorithmic variants clarify when and why distillation helps.

papers_seen.author: Shaffer
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation has emerged as a powerful paradigm for model compression and knowledge transfer in deep learning and natural language processing. This survey synthesizes current approaches to distillation, covering compression of diverse architectures including transformers, vision models, and generative models. Key developments include data-free distillation methods, multi-teacher frameworks, and task-aware approaches. Applications span NLP tasks, computer vision, and specialized domains such as medical imaging and fake media detection. The field demonstrates that compact student models can achieve performance comparable to or exceeding their non-compressed counterparts while significantly reducing computational and memory requirements.

papers_seen.author: Davidson
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses large models into smaller, faster models by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from a teacher to a student. Across vision, language, graph, generative, and neural-architecture-search settings, methods vary from matching soft labels to aligning intermediate features, using attention-based layer projection, contrastive alignment, and optimization-aware divergences. Practical adaptations address data availability, privacy, and efficiency constraints, while empirical and theoretical analyses reveal optimization limits, dataset and heterogeneity sensitivities, and opportunities from meta-learning teachers and task-specific design. Despite broad success, key open problems remain in reliably preserving teacher knowledge, designing data- and privacy-aware protocols, and tailoring distillation to domain-specific structures.

papers_seen.author: Hahn
papers_seen.title: PKD: General Distillation Framework for Object Detectors via Pearson Correlation Coefficient
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation(KD) is a widely-used technique to train compact models in object detection. However, there is still a lack of study on how to distill between heterogeneous detectors. In this paper, we empirically find that better FPN features from a heterogeneous teacher detector can help the student although their detection heads and label assignments are different. However, directly aligning the feature maps to distill detectors suffers from two problems. First, the difference in feature magnitude between the teacher and the student could enforce overly strict constraints on the student. Second, the FPN stages and channels with large feature magnitude from the teacher model could dominate the gradient of distillation loss, which will overwhelm the effects of other features in KD and introduce much noise. To address the above issues, we propose to imitate features with Pearson Correlation Coefficient to focus on the relational information from the teacher and relax constraints on the magnitude of the features. Our method consistently outperforms the existing detection KD methods and works for both homogeneous and heterogeneous student-teacher pairs. Furthermore, it converges faster. With a powerful MaskRCNN-Swin detector as the teacher, ResNet-50 based RetinaNet and FCOS achieve 41.5% and 43.9% mAP on COCO2017, which are 4.1\% and 4.8\% higher than the baseline, respectively.

papers_seen.author: Liu
papers_seen.title: Enabling Multimodal Generation on CLIP via Vision-Language Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: The recent large-scale vision-language pre-training (VLP) of dual-stream architectures (e.g., CLIP) with a tremendous amount of image-text pair data, has shown its superiority on various multimodal alignment tasks. Despite its success, the resulting models are not capable of multimodal generative tasks due to the weak text encoder. To tackle this problem, we propose to augment the dual-stream VLP model with a textual pre-trained language model (PLM) via vision-language knowledge distillation (VLKD), enabling the capability for multimodal generation. VLKD is pretty data- and computation-efficient compared to the pre-training from scratch. Experimental results show that the resulting model has strong zero-shot performance on multimodal generation tasks, such as open-ended visual question answering and image captioning. For example, it achieves 44.5% zero-shot accuracy on the VQAv2 dataset, surpassing the previous state-of-the-art zero-shot model with $7\times$ fewer parameters. Furthermore, the original textual language understanding and generation ability of the PLM is maintained after VLKD, which makes our model versatile for both multimodal and unimodal tasks.

papers_seen.author: Wood
papers_seen.title: What Makes a "Good" Data Augmentation in Knowledge Distillation -- A Statistical Perspective
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a general neural network training approach that uses a teacher model to guide the student model. Existing works mainly study KD from the network output side (e.g., trying to design a better KD loss function), while few have attempted to understand it from the input side. Especially, its interplay with data augmentation (DA) has not been well understood. In this paper, we ask: Why do some DA schemes (e.g., CutMix) inherently perform much better than others in KD? What makes a "good" DA in KD? Our investigation from a statistical perspective suggests that a good DA scheme should reduce the covariance of the teacher-student cross-entropy. A practical metric, the stddev of teacher's mean probability (T. stddev), is further presented and well justified empirically. Besides the theoretical understanding, we also introduce a new entropy-based data-mixing DA scheme, CutMixPick, to further enhance CutMix. Extensive empirical studies support our claims and demonstrate how we can harvest considerable performance gains simply by using a better DA scheme in knowledge distillation.

papers_seen.author: Fowler
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Recent Approaches
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has emerged as a central technique for compressing large deep models into smaller, more efficient students while retaining much of the teachers' performance. Recent work expands the KD toolkit beyond matching soft logits to include feature- and layer-level mimicry, task-aware selection of teacher knowledge, data-free and multi-teacher strategies, and augmentation-driven improvements. Practical advances target domain-specific challenges in language models and cross-modal systems, emphasize efficient training and deployment on heterogeneous hardware, and reinterpret KD as a form of regularization that can sometimes be partially replaced or simulated. This review synthesizes these directions and highlights recurring design principles for effective distillation in both NLP and general deep learning settings.

papers_seen.author: Pacheco
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation with Adversarial Samples Supporting Decision Boundary
papers_seen.abstract: Many recent works on knowledge distillation have provided ways to transfer the knowledge of a trained network for improving the learning process of a new one, but finding a good technique for knowledge distillation is still an open problem. In this paper, we provide a new perspective based on a decision boundary, which is one of the most important component of a classifier. The generalization performance of a classifier is closely related to the adequacy of its decision boundary, so a good classifier bears a good decision boundary. Therefore, transferring information closely related to the decision boundary can be a good attempt for knowledge distillation. To realize this goal, we utilize an adversarial attack to discover samples supporting a decision boundary. Based on this idea, to transfer more accurate information about the decision boundary, the proposed algorithm trains a student classifier based on the adversarial samples supporting the decision boundary. Experiments show that the proposed method indeed improves knowledge distillation and achieves the state-of-the-arts performance.

papers_seen.author: Reid
papers_seen.title: Moonshine: Distilling with Cheap Convolutions
papers_seen.abstract: Many engineers wish to deploy modern neural networks in memory-limited settings; but the development of flexible methods for reducing memory use is in its infancy, and there is little knowledge of the resulting cost-benefit. We propose structural model distillation for memory reduction using a strategy that produces a student architecture that is a simple transformation of the teacher architecture: no redesign is needed, and the same hyperparameters can be used. Using attention transfer, we provide Pareto curves/tables for distillation of residual networks with four benchmark datasets, indicating the memory versus accuracy payoff. We show that substantial memory savings are possible with very little loss of accuracy, and confirm that distillation provides student network performance that is better than training that student architecture directly on data.

papers_seen.author: Calderon
papers_seen.title: Learning Generalizable Models for Vehicle Routing Problems via Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Recent neural methods for vehicle routing problems always train and test the deep models on the same instance distribution (i.e., uniform). To tackle the consequent cross-distribution generalization concerns, we bring the knowledge distillation to this field and propose an Adaptive Multi-Distribution Knowledge Distillation (AMDKD) scheme for learning more generalizable deep models. Particularly, our AMDKD leverages various knowledge from multiple teachers trained on exemplar distributions to yield a light-weight yet generalist student model. Meanwhile, we equip AMDKD with an adaptive strategy that allows the student to concentrate on difficult distributions, so as to absorb hard-to-master knowledge more effectively. Extensive experimental results show that, compared with the baseline neural methods, our AMDKD is able to achieve competitive results on both unseen in-distribution and out-of-distribution instances, which are either randomly synthesized or adopted from benchmark datasets (i.e., TSPLIB and CVRPLIB). Notably, our AMDKD is generic, and consumes less computational resources for inference.

papers_seen.author: Ellis
papers_seen.title: On Representation Knowledge Distillation for Graph Neural Networks
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a learning paradigm for boosting resource-efficient graph neural networks (GNNs) using more expressive yet cumbersome teacher models. Past work on distillation for GNNs proposed the Local Structure Preserving loss (LSP), which matches local structural relationships defined over edges across the student and teacher's node embeddings. This paper studies whether preserving the global topology of how the teacher embeds graph data can be a more effective distillation objective for GNNs, as real-world graphs often contain latent interactions and noisy edges. We propose Graph Contrastive Representation Distillation (G-CRD), which uses contrastive learning to implicitly preserve global topology by aligning the student node embeddings to those of the teacher in a shared representation space. Additionally, we introduce an expanded set of benchmarks on large-scale real-world datasets where the performance gap between teacher and student GNNs is non-negligible. Experiments across 4 datasets and 14 heterogeneous GNN architectures show that G-CRD consistently boosts the performance and robustness of lightweight GNNs, outperforming LSP (and a global structure preserving variant of LSP) as well as baselines from 2D computer vision. An analysis of the representational similarity among teacher and student embedding spaces reveals that G-CRD balances preserving local and global relationships, while structure preserving approaches are best at preserving one or the other. Our code is available at https://github.com/chaitjo/efficient-gnns

papers_seen.author: Roman
papers_seen.title: Fair Feature Distillation for Visual Recognition
papers_seen.abstract: Fairness is becoming an increasingly crucial issue for computer vision, especially in the human-related decision systems. However, achieving algorithmic fairness, which makes a model produce indiscriminative outcomes against protected groups, is still an unresolved problem. In this paper, we devise a systematic approach which reduces algorithmic biases via feature distillation for visual recognition tasks, dubbed as MMD-based Fair Distillation (MFD). While the distillation technique has been widely used in general to improve the prediction accuracy, to the best of our knowledge, there has been no explicit work that also tries to improve fairness via distillation. Furthermore, We give a theoretical justification of our MFD on the effect of knowledge distillation and fairness. Throughout the extensive experiments, we show our MFD significantly mitigates the bias against specific minorities without any loss of the accuracy on both synthetic and real-world face datasets.

papers_seen.author: Zuniga
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Flexible Core for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, versatile approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable ones across modalities. When combined with complementary techniques—such as self-supervised teacher-to-student transfer, data-aware augmentation, progressive module replacement, architecture search, pruning, quantization, curriculum strategies, and teacher optimization—KD delivers strong accuracy/efficiency trade-offs while addressing constraints like privacy and data unavailability. This paper argues that KD should be treated not as a single recipe but as a composable framework that can be adapted to task, data, and hardware requirements to maximize utility in real-world NLP and deep-learning deployments.

papers_seen.author: Osborne
papers_seen.title: Distilling Knowledge from Deep Networks with Applications to Healthcare Domain
papers_seen.abstract: Exponential growth in Electronic Healthcare Records (EHR) has resulted in new opportunities and urgent needs for discovery of meaningful data-driven representations and patterns of diseases in Computational Phenotyping research. Deep Learning models have shown superior performance for robust prediction in computational phenotyping tasks, but suffer from the issue of model interpretability which is crucial for clinicians involved in decision-making. In this paper, we introduce a novel knowledge-distillation approach called Interpretable Mimic Learning, to learn interpretable phenotype features for making robust prediction while mimicking the performance of deep learning models. Our framework uses Gradient Boosting Trees to learn interpretable features from deep learning models such as Stacked Denoising Autoencoder and Long Short-Term Memory. Exhaustive experiments on a real-world clinical time-series dataset show that our method obtains similar or better performance than the deep learning models, and it provides interpretable phenotypes for clinical decision making.

papers_seen.author: Ramirez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and Natural Language Processing
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation has emerged as a powerful technique for model compression and knowledge transfer in deep learning and NLP. By training a lightweight student network to mimic a larger, well-trained teacher network, this approach enables the deployment of high-performance models on resource-constrained devices while maintaining competitive accuracy. Knowledge distillation operates through the transfer of soft targets and intermediate representations from teacher to student networks, providing implicit regularization and accelerating convergence. The technique has been successfully applied across diverse domains including computer vision, machine translation, information retrieval, and speech processing, offering substantial reductions in model size and computational cost with minimal performance degradation.

papers_seen.author: Ryan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge distillation from multi-modal to mono-modal segmentation networks
papers_seen.abstract: The joint use of multiple imaging modalities for medical image segmentation has been widely studied in recent years. The fusion of information from different modalities has demonstrated to improve the segmentation accuracy, with respect to mono-modal segmentations, in several applications. However, acquiring multiple modalities is usually not possible in a clinical setting due to a limited number of physicians and scanners, and to limit costs and scan time. Most of the time, only one modality is acquired. In this paper, we propose KD-Net, a framework to transfer knowledge from a trained multi-modal network (teacher) to a mono-modal one (student). The proposed method is an adaptation of the generalized distillation framework where the student network is trained on a subset (1 modality) of the teacher's inputs (n modalities). We illustrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework in brain tumor segmentation with the BraTS 2018 dataset. Using different architectures, we show that the student network effectively learns from the teacher and always outperforms the baseline mono-modal network in terms of segmentation accuracy.

papers_seen.author: Brown
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a widely-used technique in deep learning that enables the transfer of knowledge from large, complex teacher models to smaller, more efficient student models. This approach facilitates model compression without significant performance degradation, making it highly valuable for deploying neural networks in resource-constrained environments. Knowledge distillation has been successfully applied across diverse domains including computer vision, natural language processing, and reinforcement learning, with various methodological innovations improving its effectiveness and applicability.

papers_seen.author: Clark
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related compression techniques transform large, expensive models into smaller, faster, or otherwise more deployable models by transferring knowledge from one model (teacher) to another (student). Research over the past decade has produced a spectrum of methods: representation- and layer-matching, soft-target regularization and teacher-free variants, data-free and adversarial sample synthesis, many-to-many layer alignment for transformer compression, and task-adaptive architecture search with distillation objectives. These approaches address practical constraints—limited compute, privacy of training data, heterogeneous devices, and task-specific requirements—while revealing theoretical connections between KD and regularization. Empirical work shows KD is effective across vision and language tasks, can enable competitive small models for NLP, and remains central to specialized pipelines such as non-autoregressive translation and transformer pruning. Open directions include better matching of inductive biases between teacher and student, principled handling of data absence or privacy, and automated, task-aware compression strategies.

papers_seen.author: Reid
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression: Essential Techniques for Deploying Deep Learning and NLP Models at Scale
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and model compression have emerged as critical techniques for enabling the deployment of sophisticated deep learning models in resource-constrained environments. These methods allow large, high-performing teacher models to transfer their learned knowledge to smaller, more efficient student models, addressing the computational and memory limitations that prevent state-of-the-art systems from reaching practical applications. This survey examines the theoretical foundations, diverse applications, and ongoing innovations in these compression techniques across computer vision and natural language processing domains.

The field has evolved to encompass diverse methodologies, from basic logit matching to advanced layer-wise and feature-level distillation approaches, with applications spanning machine translation, question answering, sentiment analysis, and multi-modal learning.'}, {'author': 'Walter', 'year': 2017, 'title': 'Knowledge Distillation from A Stronger Teacher', 'abstract': 'Unlike existing knowledge distillation methods focus on the baseline settings, where the teacher models and training strategies are not that strong and competing as state-of-the-art approaches, this paper presents a method dubbed DIST to distill better from a stronger teacher. Open directions include better matching of inductive biases between teacher and student, principled handling of data absence or privacy, and automated, task-aware compression strategies.'}, {'author': 'Reid', 'year': 2023, 'title': 'Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression: Essential Techniques for Deploying Deep Learning and NLP Models at Scale', 'abstract': 'Knowledge distillation and model compression have emerged as critical techniques for enabling the deployment of sophisticated deep learning models in resource-constrained environments. These methods allow large, high-performing teacher models to transfer their learned knowledge to smaller, more efficient student models, addressing the computational and memory limitations that prevent state-of-the-art systems from reaching practical applications.
